In the Hyades this sorting is well measured, so the faint members a bright Moon removes are mostly from the cluster's outskirts. The heart of the V, drawn in its heaviest and brightest members, is exactly what survives.

M44.beat: A crowd: the glow that vanishes
M44.question: Why does the Beehive disappear to your eye tonight but not in binoculars?
M44.why: To the naked eye on a dark night the Beehive is a soft smudge, the blended light of many stars, and that makes it a perfect experiment for a moonlit sky.
M44.look: Look midway between Pollux and Regulus, in faint Cancer. By eye the smudge is probably gone tonight; in binoculars dozens of white and pale-yellow stars are still there, in little triangles and pairs.
M44.answer: By eye you saw the cluster’s combined glow, light spread thinly over a patch wider than the Moon, and the moonlit sky drowns it. Binoculars split that glow back into separate points, and points are what the Moon cannot hide.
M44.story: Until the telescope, the Beehive was known only as a small cloud, and Galileo was the first to see it break into stars, about forty of them, in 1610. Every cluster that looks like a soft patch to the naked eye is the same kind of illusion, a crowd of points too close together and too faint for the eye to separate. That blended glow is precisely the form of light moonlight steals.

Mel111.beat: A crowd: a loose near family
Mel111.question: Why does the Coma Star Cluster stay visible when fainter clusters vanish?
Mel111.why: The Coma Star Cluster is a loose sprawl of stars so close that each member is fairly bright, which matters more than anything else on a moonlit night.
Mel111.look: Look between Denebola and Cor Caroli. Binoculars show a sprawl of white stars across most of the field, sparser than on a dark night but unmistakable; the orange star at its northern edge is a foreground star.
Mel111.answer: Its members are near enough to look bright one by one, and each bright point stands above the moonlit sky by itself. A cluster whose stars were too faint to see singly would have only its blended glow to offer, and that would be lost.
Mel111.story: Imagine the Coma Star Cluster ten times farther away: each star would look a hundred times fainter, and the family would shrink to a patch a tenth as wide, a faint smudge a bright Moon would erase. Nearness is what turns its ordinary stars into separate points, and points are what the Moon cannot hide.

Mel20.beat: A crowd: a near family around Mirfak
Mel20.question: Why does the Alpha Persei Cluster look nearly as rich tonight as ever?
Mel20.why: The Alpha Persei Cluster is a near family spread around Mirfak, bright enough member by member to make it one of the best clusters for a moonlit night.
Mel20.look: Center Mirfak, the brightest star of Perseus, and dozens of blue-white stars spread around it in curving chains. Tonight the faintest have gone, but the chains are still clear.
Mel20.answer: Its stars are close enough to look bright individually, so most of them stand well above the moonlit sky. Only the faintest members drop out, which leaves the cluster’s pattern almost intact.
Mel20.story: The curving chains that the eye traces through this cluster are partly the eye's own invention, since the brain links bright points into lines and arcs wherever it can, which is how every constellation was born. With the faintest members gone there are fewer points to link, so on a moonlit night the chains can look cleaner than ever.

NGC869.beat: A crowd: a far family, thinned
NGC869.question: Why does h Persei lose so many stars to the Moon when Mirfak’s cluster loses few?
NGC869.why: h Persei is the richer half of the Double Cluster, a family thousands of light-years away, and its distance decides how it fares tonight.
NGC869.look: Sweep from Cassiopeia’s W toward Perseus to the two knots of the Double Cluster. The western one, h Persei, still shows a few dozen points tonight, but the fine grain of fainter stars that fills it on a dark night is mostly gone.
NGC869.answer: Its distance is to blame: seen from about 7,400 light-years, even powerful stars look faint, and faint points sink below the moonlit glow. A nearer family like the Alpha Persei Cluster keeps far more of its members.
NGC869.story: In a cluster this far away, the line the Moon draws runs through the middle of the family: the hot giants at the top stay, and ordinary blue-white members, each still far more powerful than the Sun, drop below it. Every family loses its smallest members first, so a moonlit view leaves a cluster looking younger and more brilliant than it really is.

NGC884.question: Why do the orange stars in χ Persei still show in moonlight?
NGC884.why: χ Persei, the eastern half of the Double Cluster, has a few orange supergiants among its blue-white members, and they stand out on a moonlit night.
NGC884.look: Keep both halves of the Double Cluster in the field and turn to χ Persei, the eastern one. Its orange-tinted stars are still there among the remaining blue-white points; defocus a touch to judge their color.
NGC884.answer: The orange stars are among the most luminous in the cluster, so they stay well above the moonlit sky while fainter members fade. Their color reaches you untouched, because the Moon adds glow, not tint.
NGC884.story: Orange supergiants are rare even in rich clusters, because a heavy star spends only a short final chapter of its life in that swollen state, and a cluster of the right age catches just a few of them at once. One of the clocks astronomers use to date the Double Cluster is the number and color of exactly these stars, the members most likely to outlast any Moon.

M7.question: Why can Ptolemy’s Cluster look cleaner under a bright Moon than on a dark night?
M7.why: Ptolemy’s Cluster sits on one of the richest stretches of the Milky Way, and the Moon changes how the cluster stands out from that background.
M7.look: From Shaula, go about five degrees north-east to Ptolemy’s Cluster, a big scatter of stars in Scorpius. Tonight the rich Milky Way glow behind it has faded, and its brightest members stand out crisply with chains, pairs and a yellowish star near the middle.
M7.answer: On a dark night the cluster competes with a crowd of faint Milky Way stars behind it; moonlight removes that background, along with the cluster’s own faintest members. What is left is mostly the cluster’s bright core of stars, a cleaner if sparser view.
M7.story: Star families are made with a handful of heavyweights and a great many small stars, a pattern Edwin Salpeter first measured in 1955 by counting how many stars of each mass a group contains. The few bright stars carry most of a cluster's light, so a bright Moon can take the majority of Ptolemy's members while leaving most of its light, and its shape, in place.

M6.question: Why does BM Scorpii, the orange star of the Butterfly Cluster, still stand out tonight?
M6.why: The Butterfly Cluster is a young cluster with one orange giant on its wingtip, and the Moon’s cut shows which kind of member keeps its place.
M6.look: From Shaula, go about five degrees north to the Butterfly Cluster in Scorpius. Fewer stars than on a dark night trace its butterfly wings, but on one wingtip BM Scorpii still glows clearly orange among blue-white members.
M6.answer: BM Scorpii is one of the brightest members, so it stays well above the moonlit sky, and the Moon adds no color to wash out its orange. The fainter members that shape the wings are the ones that thin out.
M6.story: The butterfly that gives this cluster its name was traced by observers under dark skies, linking bright and faint members alike into wings. A moonlit sky removes the faint links first, so the wings thin to a few bright chains while the brightest stars hold their places. A shape drawn in stars lasts only as long as the dimmest star it depends on.

M41.beat: A crowd: thinned to its brightest
M41.question: What is left of M41 when the Moon takes its faint stars?
M41.why: M41, just south of Sirius, is a rich cluster of stars of many brightnesses, so the Moon shows clearly how a family is cut down to its brightest.
M41.look: Put Sirius at the top of the field and move about four degrees straight south. M41 is still there tonight as a smaller scatter of stars, with the orange star near its middle still visible.
M41.answer: Its brightest members remain, the orange giant among them, because each is a point that stands above the moonlit glow. The fainter stars, and the soft haze they make together, sink below it.
M41.story: A bright Moon acts on a cluster just as distance does: lifting the dimmest star you can see by a magnitude or two removes the members that would vanish if the cluster were a few times farther away. Astronomers use the reverse of this idea to measure cluster distances, matching a cluster's stars against a nearby family whose distance is known. Tonight the Moon has, in effect, moved M41 deeper into space.

M47.beat: A crowd beside a fading neighbor
M47.question: Why does M47 survive the Moon while M46 next door nearly vanishes?
M47.why: M47 and M46 sit side by side in Puppis, one a scatter of bright stars and the other a misty swarm of faint ones, a contrast built for a moonlit night.
M47.look: Center M47, a coarse scatter of bright blue-white stars about the width of the full Moon. Then look just over a degree east for M46, a fine misty patch on dark nights; tonight it is faint at best, or gone.
M47.answer: M47’s stars look bright one by one and stand above the moonlit sky, while M46 is about three times farther away and its stars blur into a faint glow. Moonlight takes the glow and leaves the points.
M47.story: Whether a cluster reaches you as points or as a glow depends on the instrument as much as on the cluster. A telescope with wider lenses would split its neighbor's haze into many faint stars and rescue some of them from the Moon, while the naked eye turns even M47 into a single soft patch. Binoculars sit in between, which is why these two clusters land on opposite sides of tonight's line.

NGC6231.question: How does a cluster this far away keep its stars in moonlight?
NGC6231.why: NGC 6231 lies thousands of light-years away, yet it is full of some of the most powerful stars known, which makes it an exception worth seeing on a moonlit night.
NGC6231.look: Follow Scorpius’s tail down to the pair ζ¹ and ζ² Scorpii, then go half a degree north to a compact knot of a dozen bright stars. They are still clear tonight, though the fainter stars between them have faded.
NGC6231.answer: What counts is how bright a star looks, and NGC 6231’s members are so powerful that even from about 5,200 light-years they shine as clear points. The Moon cares about brightness at your eye, not about distance.
NGC6231.story: A star like the Sun, moved to this cluster's distance, would be far beyond any binoculars even on the darkest night, while the heaviest stars here could be pushed farther still and remain in view. Power, not nearness, is what puts this distant family above the Moon's cut, and its light even survives a long passage through dusty space that dims it several times over.

IC2602.beat: A crowd: the Southern Pleiades, counted
IC2602.question: How many stars of the Southern Pleiades can you count tonight?
IC2602.why: The Southern Pleiades are a near family of blue-white stars around Theta Carinae, and counting them under the Moon shows the cut moonlight makes.
IC2602.look: Find Theta Carinae, the brightest of a small spray of stars just south of the Carina Nebula. The naked eye catches a few; binoculars show a spray of mostly blue-white stars, fewer than the two or three dozen of a dark night.
IC2602.answer: You count fewer, because the faintest members no longer stand above the moonlit sky. The brightest stars, near enough to look bright one by one, keep the family’s shape.
IC2602.story: Counting the stars of a familiar cluster is one of the oldest ways to grade a night's sky: the more members you can count, the darker the sky. The count falls steeply as the sky brightens, because the faint members far outnumber the bright ones, so losing even one step on the magnitude scale costs more stars than all the brighter steps together hold.

NGC3532.beat: A crowd: chains against a faded river
NGC3532.question: Why does the Wishing Well Cluster look sparser but sharper under the Moon?
NGC3532.why: The Wishing Well Cluster is a rich swarm set against the southern Milky Way, and the Moon changes both the cluster and its background.
NGC3532.look: From the Carina Nebula, move about three degrees east-north-east. Binoculars show an elongated swarm with curving chains and a few yellow-orange stars; tonight the faintest stars are gone and the Milky Way glow behind it is subdued.
NGC3532.answer: The Moon removes the faintest members and the soft background glow at the same time, so the brightest stars stand out against a plainer sky. The cluster looks smaller, but each surviving star is crisp.
NGC3532.story: Under a bright Moon a cluster looks much as it would from farther away, because raising the faintest visible star removes the same members that distance would remove first. Astronomers turn that idea around to measure cluster distances, sliding a cluster's stars up and down in brightness until they match a nearby family at a known distance. In effect, the Wishing Well has been pushed deeper into space for the night.

IC2391.question: Why does the Omicron Velorum Cluster hold up so well to a bright Moon?
IC2391.why: The Omicron Velorum Cluster is a near family, so even its modest stars look bright, which is exactly what a moonlit night rewards.
IC2391.look: It lies less than two degrees north of Delta Velorum, a corner of the False Cross. Binoculars show a loose, sparkling group of bright stars around Omicron Velorum, barely diminished by the moonlight.
IC2391.answer: At about 490 light-years its stars look bright one by one, and each stands as a point above the moonlit sky. Nearness turns ordinary stars into Moon-proof ones.
IC2391.story: A near cluster spreads its members over a wide patch of sky, which would be a weakness if it had to survive as a glow, because its light per patch is tiny. It does not need to: its stars are bright enough to stand one by one, and the Moon judges each point on its own. The farther away a cluster lies, the more it relies on the blended glow that moonlight erases.

NGC2451.beat: A crowd beside a fading neighbor
NGC2451.question: Why does NGC 2451 survive the Moon while NGC 2477 beside it fades?
NGC2451.why: NGC 2451 and NGC 2477 share a binocular field in Puppis, a bold scatter of bright stars next to a dense, misty swarm, so one view shows both sides of the Moon’s cut.
NGC2451.look: Binoculars show a loose spray of bright stars around the orange giant c Puppis. About one and a half degrees east-south-east, NGC 2477’s misty glow is faint at best tonight.
NGC2451.answer: NGC 2451’s members are near and bright, so they stay separate points above the moonlit sky. NGC 2477’s stars are far fainter and merge into a dim glow, which the Moon drowns.
NGC2451.story: The neighboring cluster is old and rich, and its heaviest stars died long ago, so its light comes from a great many modest stars, none bright enough at its distance to stand alone. A young, near family like NGC 2451 is the opposite, with its light concentrated in a few bright members. How a family's light is shared out among its stars decides how it fares under the Moon.

NGC2516.beat: A crowd: the haze goes first
NGC2516.question: What does the Moon take from the Southern Beehive?
NGC2516.why: The Southern Beehive is a handful of bright stars over a fainter haze of members, two layers that react very differently to moonlight.
NGC2516.look: In Carina, binoculars resolve a patch the width of the full Moon, a few brighter stars in a rough box. Tonight the fainter haze of members behind them is thin or gone.
NGC2516.answer: The Moon takes the haze, the blended light of members too faint to see one by one, and leaves the box of bright stars. The cluster is still there, reduced to the members that are points in their own right.
NGC2516.story: The haze you lose tonight is not a nebula but the cluster's own faint members, blended because each is too dim to register on its own; the eye adds up their light over a small patch and reports a glow. Star counts show that most of the cluster's stars are of this faint kind, so on a moonlit night the Southern Beehive keeps only a small fraction of its members, though most of its light.

NGC4755.beat: A crowd beside a vanished Coalsack
NGC4755.question: Why does the Jewel Box still sparkle while the Coalsack beside it disappears?
NGC4755.why: The Jewel Box sits just beside the Coalsack, a dark cloud seen only as a hole in the Milky Way, so this one field shows a bright crowd and a dark one reacting to the Moon.
NGC4755.look: Start at Mimosa and nudge just over a degree south-east to a compact clump shaped like a letter A, mostly blue-white with one orange star. The Coalsack’s dark patch beside the Cross is much harder to see tonight.
NGC4755.answer: The Jewel Box’s brightest members are points above the moonlit sky, and its orange star keeps its color. The Coalsack is visible only as a gap in the Milky Way’s glow, and once moonlight drowns that glow, there is nothing for the gap to show against.
NGC4755.story: For centuries the dark patches of the Milky Way were taken for gaps in the stars. It took E. E. Barnard's photographs in the early twentieth century to convince astronomers that they are clouds of dust standing in front of the starlight. Dust dims and reddens whatever lies behind it, so the Coalsack is a shadow cast on a glow, and a shadow can only be seen while there is light around it.

AST-OrionBelt.beat: A crowd: the Belt’s family, thinned
AST-OrionBelt.question: What happens to the chain of stars winding through Orion’s Belt in moonlight?
AST-OrionBelt.why: Orion’s Belt is three bright stars set in a loose young family of fainter ones, so it shows how a group is pared down to its brightest.
AST-OrionBelt.look: Put the middle Belt star in the center and let the outer two sit near the edges. The S-shaped chain of fainter stars winding through the field is thinner tonight, while the three blue-white Belt stars are untouched.
AST-OrionBelt.answer: The faint members of the chain sink below the moonlit sky, and the three Belt stars, far brighter, stay. The family is the same; the Moon simply shows you only its brightest children.
AST-OrionBelt.story: Nature makes stars the way it makes pebbles on a beach, a few big ones and a great many small, and Edwin Salpeter put numbers to that in 1955 by counting the stars of each mass near the Sun. Few as they are, the heavyweights give out most of a young group's light, so the Moon can remove most of the Belt family's members while taking only a small share of its total glow.

NGC2244.question: Why can you see the Rosette Cluster tonight but not the Rosette Nebula?
NGC2244.why: The Rosette is a young cluster wrapped in a faint ring of glowing gas, and the Moon separates the two cleanly.
NGC2244.look: Go about a third of the way from Betelgeuse to Procyon and drop slightly south into Monoceros. A small rectangle of stars stands out, one of them yellow-orange; the faint ring of haze around it, glimpsed on very dark nights, is gone.
NGC2244.answer: The cluster’s stars are points that stand above the moonlit sky, while the nebula’s glow is spread over a patch wider than the Moon and sinks below it. Points survive, thin glows do not.
NGC2244.story: The Rosette's gas glows mostly in the deep red light of hydrogen, a color the rods that run night vision hardly register, so the ring is hard to see even on a dark night. Observers who chase it fit filters that pass only the nebula's few colors and block most other light, moonlight included, a trick that can rescue some nebulae even on bright nights. The cluster's stars, shining in every color at once, need no such help.

NGC2362.beat: A crowd around one bright star
NGC2362.question: Why does τ Canis Majoris stay bright while its little cluster fades?
NGC2362.why: τ Canis Majoris is a bright star wrapped in a tiny knot of faint cluster members, the Moon’s cut squeezed into a few arcminutes.
NGC2362.look: Find Wezen and Aludra in the Great Dog’s hindquarters, south-east of Sirius. τ Canis Majoris sits about three degrees north of the point midway between them, a bright star whose faint surrounding knot is barely there tonight.
NGC2362.answer: τ Canis Majoris is a single bright point far above the moonlit glow, while the cluster members around it are faint and close together, blending into a dim haze the Moon drowns.
NGC2362.story: Inside your binoculars every glass surface scatters a little of a bright star's light, and your eye adds its own scatter, so a brilliant star always sits in a small haze of its own making. In a cluster as compact as this one the faint members live inside that haze, and on a moonlit night they must outshine two glows at once.

Cr69.beat: A crowd: a compact bright triangle
Cr69.question: Why does the λ Orionis Cluster survive the Moon when so much of Orion fades?
Cr69.why: The λ Orionis Cluster is a neat little triangle of stars at Orion’s head, with no visible nebula to lose, so it shows what a crowd of points keeps.
Cr69.look: Aim at the faint star that marks Orion’s head, above and between Betelgeuse and Bellatrix. Binoculars turn it into a neat little triangle with fainter stars around it; the triangle is clear tonight, the faintest stars thinner.
Cr69.answer: Its main stars are bright points that stand above the moonlit sky, and the faint ring of gas around them is beyond binoculars on any night, so the Moon has no nebula here to take. Only its faintest members drop out.
Cr69.story: Your eye adds up light for only about a tenth of a second before starting afresh, while a camera can add it up for minutes. That is why photographs show a vast, faint ring of glowing gas around this cluster that binoculars never show, even on the darkest night. It is also why the Moon's glow, which the camera adds up too, spoils long exposures as surely as it spoils the view. For the eye, the cluster has only ever been its stars.

M39.beat: A crowd: counted against a faded river
M39.question: How many of M39’s stars can you count under a bright Moon?
M39.why: M39 is a loose triangle of stars in the Milky Way of Cygnus, few enough to count, which makes the Moon’s effect easy to measure.
M39.look: From Deneb, sweep about 9° east-north-east to a loose triangle of stars about the size of the full Moon. Count the members at low power; tonight the Milky Way glow around it is subdued and the faintest members are missing.
M39.answer: You count fewer than on a dark night, because only the brighter white stars stand above the moonlit sky. The triangle survives because its outline is drawn in bright stars.
M39.story: Looking toward Cygnus you look straight along our own spiral arm, so the sky behind M39 is packed with faint, distant stars whose light blends into the Milky Way's glow. On a dark night that backdrop crowds the cluster and blurs its edges; under the Moon the backdrop goes first, so the cluster's brighter members stand out against plainer sky even as its faint ones are lost.

NGC457.beat: A crowd: two eyes and a fading body
NGC457.question: Why do the Owl Cluster’s two eyes outlast its body under a bright Moon?
NGC457.why: The Owl Cluster is two bright stars at the end of a faint, elongated swarm, so it shows in one small field which members a moonlit sky lets you keep.
NGC457.look: Two degrees south of Ruchbah in Cassiopeia, find a pair of stars, one much brighter than the other; the bright one is φ Cassiopeiae. Those two eyes are clear tonight, while the faint spray of wings trailing from them is thin or gone.
NGC457.answer: The eyes are the brightest points in the field and stand well above the moonlit sky, while the body is made of stars about 9,000 light-years away, faint enough to sink below it. The Moon has cut the owl down to its eyes.
NGC457.story: Distance works on a cluster like a dimmer switch on every star at once: from this far away, even stars thousands of times as powerful as the Sun arrive faint. The Owl's body is built from such stars, and its eyes stand out only because one of them is either a supergiant, the most powerful kind of star, or simply a nearer star in front, a question the Moon is happy to ignore.

AST-Coathanger.beat: A crowd that is not a family
AST-Coathanger.question: Does the Moon treat the Coathanger, a chance pattern, any differently from a true cluster?
AST-Coathanger.why: The Coathanger looks like a cluster but is a chance line-up of unrelated stars, which makes it a neat test of what moonlight cares about.
AST-Coathanger.look: Sweep a little less than halfway from Albireo toward Altair, into Vulpecula: a bar of six stars with a hook of four below its middle. A couple of the hook stars look orange; the whole pattern is easy tonight.
AST-Coathanger.answer: The Moon responds only to how bright each point looks, not to whether the stars belong together. Most of the Coathanger's stars are bright enough, so the pattern survives, its faintest members a little weaker.
AST-Coathanger.story: Whether a pattern survives moonlight depends on its faintest essential star, the one without which the shape falls apart. The Coathanger's bar and hook are drawn by stars of several brightnesses, and the faintest go first, while a true cluster would lose members in exactly the same order. The Moon sorts by brightness alone; telling family from strangers needs measured distances and motions.

NGC5139.beat: A glow: millions of stars in one ball
NGC5139.question: Why does Omega Centauri survive moonlight when it is not a point at all?
NGC5139.why: Omega Centauri is a ball of millions of stars too distant to split, so it reaches your eye as a glow, and glows are the hardest things to keep in moonlight.
NGC5139.look: In Centaurus, look for a fuzzy star that never sharpens. Binoculars show a round glow brightening toward the center; tonight its edge is pulled in and the grainy halo of dark nights is gone.
NGC5139.answer: A glow survives only if it is bright patch for patch, and Omega Centauri packs so many stars into its core that the center outshines the moonlit sky. Its thinner outskirts do not, so tonight it is a ball of light trimmed to its densest part.
NGC5139.story: Omega Centauri looks so much like a fuzzy star to the naked eye that Ptolemy listed it as one, and it still carries a star's Greek letter. Edmond Halley, observing from St Helena in 1677, was the first to record that it was not a star but a glow. On a moonlit night you can see why the confusion lasted, because the Moon trims the cluster down to its starlike core.

NGC104.beat: A glow beside a vanished galaxy
NGC104.question: Why does 47 Tucanae survive the Moon while the galaxy beside it fades?
NGC104.why: 47 Tucanae sits at the edge of the Small Magellanic Cloud, a whole galaxy of stars, so one field holds the densest glow of the night and one of the thinnest.
NGC104.look: Binoculars show 47 Tucanae as a round glow brightening sharply to an intense, almost starlike core. The Small Magellanic Cloud beside it, an obvious patch on dark nights, is faint or gone tonight.
NGC104.answer: 47 Tucanae packs its light into a small ball with a blazing core, so it outshines the moonlit sky patch for patch. The Small Magellanic Cloud has far more light in total, but spread over a wide patch of sky it is too thin to compete.
NGC104.story: Every glow in the sky is judged against the same floor, the faint natural light of the sky itself, and a bright Moon raises that floor across the whole field at once. Measure outward from the center of 47 Tucanae and its light falls steeply, while the galaxy beside it is faint and nearly flat all across. Raise the floor and the cluster loses only its edges, the galaxy nearly everything.

M22.beat: A glow: a bright ancient swarm
M22.question: Why does the Sagittarius Cluster come through moonlight when most fuzzy things in Sagittarius vanish?
M22.why: The Sagittarius Cluster is a glow of countless ancient stars, one of the brightest of its kind, in a part of the sky full of nebulae that a bright Moon erases.
M22.look: From Kaus Borealis, the top of the Teapot’s lid, move about two and a half degrees north-east. The cluster is a bright, slightly oval glow, smaller than on a dark night, its faint outer parts gone; M28 nearby is much harder tonight.
M22.answer: The Sagittarius Cluster concentrates its light, with so many stars crowded into its center that each patch of it shines brighter than the moonlit sky. Smaller, fainter M28 and the nebulae around Sagittarius spread their light too thinly, and the risen sky swallows them.
M22.story: Even without a Moon the night sky is never black: atoms high in the atmosphere glow faintly as they release energy stored by sunlight during the day, a light called airglow. Airglow sets the floor against which every faint glow is judged. Moonlight raises that floor many times over, and only the densest glows, like the heart of the Sagittarius Cluster, still clear it.

M13.question: Why can’t binoculars brighten the Hercules cluster against the Moon the way they brighten a star?
M13.why: The Hercules cluster is a ball of about half a million stars that binoculars cannot split, so it arrives as a glow, and glows play by different rules.
M13.look: In the Keystone of Hercules, about a third of the way from η to ζ Herculis, the cluster is still a fuzzy ball tonight, smaller and dimmer than on a dark night. Compare it with a star of similar brightness: one a point, the other a cloud.
M13.answer: Binoculars gather more light, but they also magnify, and for a glow the two cancel: each patch of the cluster looks no brighter than it does to your eye, just like each patch of the moonlit sky. Only its dense core outshines the sky, so that is all that survives.
M13.story: Catalogs give the Hercules cluster a single magnitude close to the limit of the naked eye, but that number is its total light, as if the whole cluster were squeezed into a point. Spread over its real size, its light per patch is far fainter than a star of the same magnitude, which is why a star that bright stays crisp tonight while the cluster dims and shrinks.

M5.beat: A glow: a core without its halo
M5.question: Why does M5 shrink to a fuzzy star under a bright Moon?
M5.why: M5 is a bright core fading into a broad halo of stars, so it shows clearly which part of a glow the Moon takes.
M5.look: From Unukalhai, the brightest star in the head of Serpens, sweep about eight degrees south-west. M5 is a small fuzzy star tonight, its bright center still there and its broad halo mostly gone.
M5.answer: Its center packs enough starlight into each patch to outshine the moonlit sky, but its halo spreads the same kind of light much more thinly, and that thin light sinks below the glow.
M5.story: M5's light drops from a bright core into a broad, gentle halo, a profile astronomers measure star by star near the edge and ring by ring through the glow toward the center. A bright Moon simply draws a line across that profile: everything brighter than the risen sky stays, everything fainter goes. That is why the cluster shrinks rather than fading evenly, keeping its core while losing its edge.

M3.beat: A glow at the edge of moonlight
M3.question: Is M3 the faintest thing the Moon leaves you tonight?
M3.why: M3 is a glow of hundreds of thousands of stars far out in the galaxy’s halo, faint enough that a bright Moon puts it right at the edge of sight.
M3.look: Aim a little past halfway from Cor Caroli toward Arcturus. M3 is a small round glow beside a yellowish field star, fainter and tighter than on a dark night; brace the binoculars and give it a patient look.
M3.answer: It is close to the limit: its core packs just enough light into each patch to rise above the moonlit sky, while everything thinner around it is lost. Galaxies and faint nebulae, spread out more thinly still, do not make it at all.
M3.story: Faint glows are a job for the rods, the eye's sensitive night cells, which crowd the edge of your gaze rather than its center. Look a little to one side of M3 and it brightens and swells, a trick called averted vision, though tonight the rods are partly dazzled and have less to give than on a moonless night.

M15.beat: A glow with a blazing core
M15.question: Why does the compact Pegasus globular hold up to moonlight better than larger, brighter-looking clusters?
M15.why: The Pegasus globular is a small ball of stars whose center has collapsed into a very dense core, and density is what a glow needs on a moonlit night.
M15.look: Draw a line from θ Pegasi through Enif and continue a little over half as far again to the north-west. The cluster sits beside a faint star: one stays a sharp point, the other a small round glow with a bright center, smaller than on a dark night.
M15.answer: What matters is light per patch, not total light, and this cluster crowds its stars into a tiny, dense center that outshines the moonlit sky. A larger cluster of the same total brightness spreads its light thinner and loses more to the glow.
M15.story: The Pegasus globular's center is one of the densest places in our galaxy. Over billions of years its stars have traded energy in close passes until the core collapsed into a tiny, crowded knot, which Hubble images resolve star by star. That knot gives the cluster its bright, almost starlike heart, and tonight it is the heart, not the cluster's total light, that stands above the moonlit sky.

M2.question: Why does M2 fade more than the Pegasus globular under the same Moon?
M2.why: M2 is a ball of stars much like the Pegasus globular but less sharply concentrated, which makes the pair a direct comparison of how glows survive moonlight.
M2.look: Start at Sadalsuud, the brightest star of Aquarius, and move about five degrees north. M2 shows as a small round fuzz tonight, fainter at the edges than on a dark night; nudge the focus and real stars snap to points while M2 never does.
M2.answer: Its light is spread a little more evenly, so its center is less intense than the Pegasus globular’s, and less of it stands above the moonlit sky. The difference between the two is not their total light but how tightly each packs it.
M2.story: Astronomers describe a globular cluster's shape by how quickly its light falls away from the center, measured by counting stars and scanning the glow ring by ring outward. Ivan King's fits in the 1960s gave every cluster a concentration, and the higher it is, the more of the light is crowded into the core, the very quantity that decides what survives a bright Moon.

NGC6752.beat: A glow with a starlike core
NGC6752.question: Why does the Peacock globular’s core survive the Moon while its halo is lost?
NGC6752.why: The Peacock globular has a core packed so tightly it looks almost like an out-of-focus star, with a faint halo around it, so it shows which part of a glow moonlight spares.
NGC6752.look: In Pavo, binoculars show an obvious round glow with a bright, concentrated core. Tonight the halo that spreads with averted vision on dark nights is missing, and the cluster looks like a fuzzy star.
NGC6752.answer: The core crowds its stars together until each patch outshines the moonlit sky, while the halo’s stars are spread too thinly to compete. Concentration, not total brightness, decides what remains.
NGC6752.story: The eye's sensitivity to a glow depends on its size as well as its brightness, because it pools light over a patch, so a large faint halo can be seen on a dark night at a contrast that would hide a small spot. Moonlight raises the bar beyond what any pooling can reach, and the Peacock's thin halo drops out. Its core, packed so tightly that it behaves almost like a star, is the part that still clears it.

M42.beat: A glow of gas with a bright heart
M42.question: How can the Orion Nebula survive a bright Moon when other nebulae vanish?
M42.why: Most nebulae are the first casualties of moonlight, but the Orion Nebula is lit from inside by a handful of very hot young stars, which gives its heart unusual brightness.
M42.look: Find the three-star Sword below Orion’s Belt; its middle star looks fuzzy even tonight. Binoculars show a bright core with stubby wings and a dark notch; the faint outer wings of dark nights are gone, and the glow looks gray.
M42.answer: Its heart, close to the hot stars that light it, is bright patch for patch, enough to rise above the moonlit sky. The outer gas is lit more weakly and spread wider, so it sinks below the glow, leaving the core like a small flame.
M42.story: A glowing cloud has a surprising property: move it farther away and it shrinks, but each patch of it stays exactly as bright. That is because the light from the patch and the area it covers both fall with the square of the distance. So the Orion Nebula's heart would face the Moon on the same terms from twice as far, only smaller, and what decides its fate is how fiercely its gas is lit, not how near it is.

M31.beat: A glow: a galaxy trimmed to its core
M31.question: Why does the Andromeda Galaxy shrink to a small smudge in moonlight?
M31.why: The Andromeda Galaxy gives off as much light in total as a fairly bright star, yet it is spread across a huge patch of sky, the clearest case of how the Moon judges light.
M31.look: From Mirach, the middle bright star of Andromeda, climb two fainter stars to the north. Tonight you will probably see only the small oval core; the haze that stretches several Moon-widths on a dark night is lost in the glare.
M31.answer: The Moon judges light patch by patch, and only Andromeda’s crowded central bulge is bright enough per patch to rise above the moonlit sky. The rest of its hundreds of billions of stars are still shining there, spread too thinly to compete tonight.
M31.story: A galaxy's light falls off steadily from its center: the bulge of old stars at Andromeda's heart is many times brighter per patch than the spiral disk around it, and the disk itself fades outward. Astronomers map that fall-off by measuring the light in rings around the center, and the map tells you how big Andromeda will look under any sky. The edge you see is simply where its falling glow meets the risen sky.

NGC3372.beat: A glow of gas, reduced to its heart
NGC3372.question: What is left of the great Carina Nebula when the Moon is up?
NGC3372.why: The Carina Nebula is the brightest nebula of the southern sky, a vast glowing cloud, so it shows how much of even a great nebula moonlight can take.
NGC3372.look: Sweep the Milky Way between the Southern Cross and the False Cross. Binoculars still show the bright heart around the small orange point of Eta Carinae, cut by a dark notch; the wide outer haze of a dark night is mostly gone.
NGC3372.answer: The heart survives, lit fiercely by the young stars buried in it and bright patch for patch. The wider cloud is lit more weakly and spread over a patch many times the Moon, so it sinks below the moonlit glow.
NGC3372.story: Much of a glowing nebula's light comes out in a few pure colors: deep red from hydrogen, to which the eye's night vision is almost blind, and a blue-green from oxygen, which it sees well. That is why big nebulae look gray-green to the eye rather than the red of photographs, and why observers fit filters that pass only those colors, cutting the moonlit sky's broad glow far more than the nebula's light.

M11.beat: A glow: a cluster too rich to split
M11.question: Why does the Wild Duck Cluster survive as a glow when sparser clusters lose their stars?
M11.why: The Wild Duck is an open cluster so rich and distant that binoculars barely split it, so its thousands of stars reach you mostly as a compact glow.
M11.look: Follow Aquila’s tail south into little Scutum, then go about two degrees south-east of β Scuti. The Wild Duck is a small, fan-shaped haze with a brighter star at its apex, more compact and less grainy than on a dark night.
M11.answer: Thousands of stars packed into a small fan make each patch of the Wild Duck brighter than the moonlit sky, even though its single stars are too faint to see one by one. A looser cluster of the same stars would spread that light too thin.
M11.story: The eye's threshold depends on size as well as brightness: Blackwell's wartime experiments showed that a large patch can be seen at a lower contrast than a small one, because the eye pools light over its area. That favors big, faint glows on dark nights, but under a bright Moon even a large patch needs real brightness per patch, and only a dense one like the Wild Duck still clears the bar.

NGC3293.beat: A glow: a compact bright knot
NGC3293.question: Why does the tiny Gem Cluster hold up to moonlight so well?
NGC3293.why: The Gem Cluster crowds its brightest stars into a patch much smaller than the Moon, the point where a crowd of stars starts to look like a glow.
NGC3293.look: From the bright heart of the Carina Nebula, move about two degrees north-west. Binoculars show a compact, bright clump with a few stars resolved around a hazy center, still clear tonight.
NGC3293.answer: Its light is packed into a very small patch, so the hazy center outshines the moonlit sky while its brightest stars stand out as points. Small and bright per patch is exactly what survives a bright Moon.
NGC3293.story: How do we know the Gem's hazy center is stars rather than gas? In 1864 William Huggins turned a spectroscope on the sky's nebulae and found two kinds: some showed the bright lines of glowing gas, others the rainbow of starlight crossed by dark lines. The Gem's mist is of the second kind, the blended light of members too faint for binoculars, and like all light spread over a patch, it is judged by the Moon patch for patch.
